walkthroughs.body_html: SA Chief Ernst Rohm demanded a 'second revolution' and integration of the Reichswehr into the SA. The army insisted on its monopoly of arms. On 30 June 1934 SS units arrested and shot Rohm and around 85 victims including Strasser and Schleicher. The army's gratitude was sealed by the Fuhrer Oath on 2 August after Hindenburg's death, when Hitler combined the offices of President and Chancellor.

Ian Kershaw's concept of 'working towards the Fuhrer' explains how subordinates anticipated Hitler's wishes without explicit orders. The state apparatus competed: party, ministries, SS, Four Year Plan office (Goring) and military overlapped. Functionalist historians like Hans Mommsen argued this polycratic dynamic produced radicalisation through cumulative initiatives rather than master plans.

The Gestapo had only 7,000 officers in 1939 but relied on informers; Robert Gellately stressed widespread denunciation. Concentration camps under Eicke's Dachau model expanded after 1934. The 1935 Reich Citizenship Law and Nazi welfare programmes (Strength Through Joy, Winter Help) blended coercion and reward. Goebbels's Ministry of Propaganda coordinated media to manufacture consent.
